title: Get Hired at YC Startups
subtitle: Get in, reach out, get hired — tech roles only.
description: Three weeks for engineers who want good / YC companies. Week 1 you shortlist on Work at a Startup and the YC directory. Week 2 you send founder notes. Week 3 you package shipped work and a take-home plan so a founding-engineer interview does not surprise you.
outcomes: Get in — 8 companies from Work at a Startup / the YC directory, with why you and what you would ship in 90 days
Reach out — 5 founder notes sent, each pointing at one shipped artifact
Get hired — a tech story bank plus a weekend take-home plan in their stack

modules.title: Week 1: Get into good / YC startups
modules.summary: Work at a Startup is the hub. You leave with a profile and a shortlist you could defend to a founder.

lessons.title: Founding Engineer at a YC Startup | Work at a Startup
lessons.description: YC’s Work at a Startup team plus three early engineers. Pause on: what founding engineer actually means, how they found the company (WAAS, founder DM, a friend), and which skills besides code they were hired for.

lessons.title: Advice for Picking the Right Startup
lessons.description: Treat the offer like a concentrated investment: learn the business, talk to people who work there, and do not pick on title. Use this to throw companies off your shortlist.

lessons.title: Outcome 1: Shortlist 8 YC / good startups
lessons.description: Fill a Work at a Startup profile, then pick eight companies you could join as an engineer this year. Watching does not count.

assignment.brief: Create or update your profile on Work at a Startup (https://www.workatastartup.com). Use the YC directory (https://www.ycombinator.com/companies) to filter by batch, industry, and hiring. Every company on the list needs a role you can actually do, a stack you can ship in, and a 90-day ship. Drop companies you cannot explain.
assignment.deliverable: A public WAAS profile plus eight companies a founder could take seriously.

fields.label: Work at a Startup profile URL
fields.hint: Fill the profile in earnest — engineers on the YC panel said founders messaged them within a day when the profile was specific.

fields.label: The stack you can ship in this month (languages, frameworks, systems)
fields.placeholder: TypeScript + Next.js + Postgres. I have shipped X. I will not claim Y.
fields.hint: Early YC teams hire generalists who can touch the product this week. Name what you can demo, not a wishlist.

fields.label: Eight companies: name, YC batch or why they are ‘good’, role, 90-day ship
fields.placeholder:
1. [Company] · [W24 / Series A / why] · [role] · In 90 days I would ship…
2. …
fields.hint: Prefer companies that are hiring engineers on WAAS. If they are not YC, say why they are still a company you would join (product, team, stage).

fields.label: Two companies you refused, and why
fields.placeholder: I passed on [company] because I cannot explain the business / I would hate the team / the role is not engineering…
fields.hint: Picking the right startup is also saying no. Use the video’s test: would you spend two years in the trenches with these people, and do you understand the business?

checklist: The WAAS profile names a stack and shipped work, not ‘passionate about startups’.
Each of the eight has a role you could do this quarter.
You can explain the business of each company in one sentence.
You cut two companies on purpose.

lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Getting into YC companies
lessons.description: How engineers actually land at good / YC startups.

questions.prompt: The official place YC companies hire engineers, and candidates apply, is:

options.text: A cold LinkedIn blast to every founder in the last three batches.
Work at a Startup (workatastartup.com) plus the YC company directory.
Only campus placement cells.
LeetCode contests — the top 1% get an automatic YC offer.

questions.explanation: WAAS is the YC hiring hub. The directory tells you who exists. Outreach is week 2, after you have a shortlist.

questions.prompt: A founding / early engineer role at a YC company is mostly:

options.text: One language, one ticket queue, no customer contact.
Shipping across the stack, plus product, customers, and culture — not just code.
The same as a Staff Engineer at a 10,000-person company.
A guaranteed CTO title after 90 days.

questions.explanation: The WAAS panel: you bleed into PM, support, and hiring. Titles are often just ‘software engineer’.

questions.prompt: When choosing which startup to join, the video’s strongest filter is:

options.text: The job title printed on the offer letter.
Whether you understand the business and would spend years with the people.
Whichever company replied to you first.
The one with the most blog posts about culture.

questions.explanation: Treat it like a concentrated investment. Learn the business. Talk to people there. Like the team — most early startups fail.

modules.title: Week 2: Reach out to them
modules.summary: Same loop founders use to get customers: list, short note, one artifact, one ask. Send it.

lessons.title: How to Sell | Startup School
lessons.description: Tyler Bosmeny’s sales craft applied to founder notes: short, personal, about them, one ask. You are not selling a product — you are asking for 20 minutes and pointing at one shipped artifact.

lessons.title: How to Get Your First Customers | Startup School
lessons.description: The list → note → demo loop. This week the ‘customer’ is a hiring founder. Build the list from WAAS DMs, founder emails on the YC directory, and people you already know. Do not wait for a careers page.

lessons.title: Outcome 2: Send five founder notes
lessons.description: Write and send five notes. A draft folder is not outreach.

assignment.brief: Pick five companies from week 1. Find the founder or hiring engineer (WAAS message, email on the YC directory, or a warm intro). Each note: why this company, one shipped artifact (PR, product URL, write-up), one ask (20 minutes or a take-home). Paste the sent text and how you sent it.
assignment.deliverable: Five notes that left your outbox, plus the artifact URL you pointed at.

fields.label: The one shipped artifact you will point every note at
fields.hint: A live URL a founder can click in 30 seconds. A résumé PDF is not an artifact.

fields.label: The best note you actually sent (subject + body)
fields.placeholder:
Subject: shipped X — relevant to [their product]

4–8 lines. Why them. The link. One ask.
fields.hint: Personal. About their product. One ask for time, not ‘any roles?’.

fields.label: The five sends: company, person, channel, date
fields.hint: If you could not send yet, write ‘queued’ and the blocker. Three of the five must be sent.

fields.label: The follow-up you will send in five days if they are silent
fields.placeholder: One new line (a commit, a user quote, a question about their product) + the same ask.
fields.hint: Do not resend the first note. Add one new fact.

checklist: A founder can click the artifact without logging in.
The note is about their company, not your GPA.
At least three notes left your outbox.
The follow-up adds a new fact.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: Outreach that gets a reply
lessons.description: What a hiring founder actually opens.

questions.prompt: The job of a first founder note is:

options.text: Attach a CV and ask if they are hiring anyone.
Get 20 minutes (or a take-home) by showing you already understand their product.
List every language you have touched since class 11.
Negotiate salary before they know your name.

questions.explanation: Same as a founder sales note: one ask, about them, with proof you did the work.

questions.prompt: The strongest thing to put in the note is:

options.text: A live PR or product URL that is relevant to what they ship.
Your CGPA and rank.
A five-page cover letter.
‘I am passionate about your mission’ with no product detail.

questions.explanation: YC engineers got replies when the profile and the note pointed at specific shipped work.

questions.prompt: If the founder does not reply, the next move is:

options.text: Send the same note daily until they block you.
Wait six months and assume they hated you.
Follow up once with one new fact (a commit, a user quote, a product question).
Post publicly that they ignored you.

questions.explanation: One new fact, same ask. Silence is normal. Spam is how you get remembered the wrong way.

modules.title: Week 3: Make sure you get hired
modules.summary: Tech-specific: story bank from shipped work, a weekend take-home plan, and questions that prove you learned the business.

lessons.title: How Startup Hiring Actually Works
lessons.description: What founders screen for: speed, judgment, and whether you have shipped. Map each point to one story from your PRs or product — not a textbook definition of ‘culture fit’.

lessons.title: Founding Engineer at a YC Startup (replay the hiring bits)
lessons.description: Skip to how the panelists interviewed and what they wish they had shown: generalist range, shipping ugly MVPs, talking to customers, and questions about the business. Rewatch with a notebook of your own stories.

lessons.title: Outcome 3: Story bank + weekend take-home plan
lessons.description: Package the proof a founding-engineer interview asks for. If they send a take-home tonight, you already know the timebox.

assignment.brief: Pick one company from week 1 you would accept. Write three stories from work you actually shipped (a PR, a product, a broken deploy). Then write the weekend take-home plan in their stack: repo, tests, README, what you will not polish. End with five questions for the founder about the business — the picking-a-startup video said almost nobody does this.
assignment.deliverable: A story bank and a take-home plan you could start tonight.

fields.label: The company you would accept, and why (business + people)
fields.placeholder: I would join [company] because the product is… and I would spend two years with…
fields.hint: Use week 1’s filter. Title and salary are not enough.

fields.label: Three shipped-work stories (problem → what you built → what broke → result)
fields.placeholder:
1. [PR/product] — problem, your change, the failure, the metric or user.
2. …
3. …
fields.hint: Founders hire people who have already shipped. Include one story where you threw work away or talked to a user.

fields.label: Weekend take-home plan in their stack
fields.placeholder:
Stack: …
Timebox: 8 hours
Must ship: README, one happy path, tests for X
Will not polish: …
How I will record a 3-min walkthrough: …
fields.hint: Early teams care that you ship a working slice with a README, not a framework tour. Name what you will refuse so you finish.

fields.label: Five questions you will ask the founder about the business
fields.placeholder:
1. Who already pays / uses this, and what they did last week…
2. What broke in the last month…
fields.hint: Business, customers, and how they decide what to build. Not ‘what is the tech stack?’ — you can read that.

checklist: Each story is from work you shipped, not a hypothetical.
The take-home has a timebox and a ‘will not polish’ list.
At least one story includes a user or a thrown-away MVP.
The founder questions are about the business, not the cafeteria.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Getting hired as an engineer
lessons.description: What actually moves a YC / early-startup hire.

questions.prompt: In a founding-engineer interview, the strongest proof is:

options.text: A story of something you shipped, including what broke.
Naming every design pattern in Gang of Four.
Saying you only want to write backend in one language.
Asking about snacks before asking about customers.

questions.explanation: Early teams hire people who have shipped and can talk about the mess. Specialists who refuse the rest of the stack are a poor early-stage fit.

questions.prompt: If they send a take-home on Friday, the move is:

options.text: Rewrite it in a new framework to impress them.
Timebox a working slice, tests for the risky part, and a README / walkthrough.
Spend the weekend on perfect CSS and skip the happy path.
Paste ChatGPT output with no repo they can run.

questions.explanation: Same as the founding-engineer panel: ship a testable slice fast. They will run it.

questions.prompt: A question that makes you look hireable at a YC company is:

options.text: ‘What is the work-life balance?’ as the first question.
‘Who is the customer, what did they do last week, and what did you throw away?’
‘Can I be CTO in three months?’
‘Do I have to talk to users?’

questions.explanation: Almost nobody does the business homework. That is the filter from the picking-a-startup talk — and it is how you decide whether to join.
